Such classification is broken into three distinct calculations: (1) urban vs. rural, (2) restricted vs. unrestricted, (3) and off-network. By comparing GPS location to the U.S. Census populated area geographic boundary shape file and determining if the point’s location was within a geographic area with a population of 5,000 or more per the Federal Highway Administration’s definition of an urban area (Federal Highway Administration 2018), we classified each point as urban or rural. The specific shape file used was found on the data.gov website and is titled “tl_2017_us_uac10.zip” (U.S. Census Bureau 2021). The 2017 TomTom U.S. road network database was used for identifying restricted, unrestricted, and off-network points by matching a given point to a part of the road network. (See Table 3 for a summary of mapping to MOVES road types.) To save computation time, the closest road link to a given point within 0.01 arc seconds was considered the matched road link.2 If no road links were within that radius, the point was considered off-network. In addition to points that did not match to any road segment, those points where the vehicle was idling for 120 seconds or longer were also classified as off- network. Idle is defined as engine speed >200 rotations per minute (RPM) and vehicle speed <1 mile per hour (mph). Once these classifications were done, each data point was given the appropriate road type number per the MOVES definitions. Note that there are differences in the road network used for the FleetDNA and CRC A-100 projects. FleetDNA used the TomTom network, whereas CRC A-100 used the U.S. Census TIGER network (DenBleyker et al. 2017). This may contribute to differences observed in the two data sets, as mentioned later. 2 At the equator, 0.1 arc seconds roughly equals 3.087 meters.
